title: Stephen G. Ware - Planning and Replanning Structured Adaptive Stories: 25 Years of History
speaker: Stephen G. Ware
talk_title: Planning and Replanning Structured Adaptive Stories: 25 Years of History
description: Emergent stories are great for games like Dwarf Fortress, but sometimes interactive stories have a required ending or structure they have to follow. In these situations, you need to plan your story in advance to anticipate the consequences of a player's choice on what is possible. Most planned stories are designed by hand (think Choose Your Own Adventure books), but there has also been 25 years of research on story planning algorithms that can rewrite a structured story while a game is running. This talk will give a short history of the challenges of representing a story as a data structure suitable for algorithmic generation, including how we model events, intentions, beliefs, conflict, and emotion. This history will be told though a series of bad stories generated by earlier systems and how those mis-spun tales motivated next steps in the research.

segments.text: STEPHEN: I am Stephen and I work at the University of Kentucky. I have always wanted to attend
Roguelike Celebration so I am excited to be here for my first time. Today I am doing a quick and
partial history of storytelling algorithms. That history starts in 1974 with tail spin and since
then people have asked can you get a computer to write a story for you although I would argue
that is not an interesting question. The word is full of people who want to tell stories. The more
interesting question is can you get a computer to rewrite a story for you? Writing a story is
fun but if you put it in a game you have to adapt this. People do this all of the time when playing
D&D. I am going to talk about how we have tried to represent a story on a computer and whether we can
automate stories fast enough. This is specifically about automated, planned, event level narratives.
I will define all the cool stuff this talk isn't going to cover. If you are into games you
are familiar with the difference between static narratives like books and films and interactive
narratives. You have a story with a player who is going to make plays you can't control. One
thing is what is considered an atomic unit. The scene level is roughly a paragraph of content in
a written story. These days large language models can write stories one token meaning one word at
a time. The algorithms I am talking about today are at the event level and an event corresponds
to about one sentence with a subject, verb, and direct objective. If you have played a scum style
game that's a narrative. You can think of it like Lego bricks, IKEA furniture and a 3d printer.
Games like dwarf and the Sims have a virtual world populated by relative many lightweight agents.
Emergent stories are unpredictable and that's part of the joy but if you have specific story
beats you have to hit you have to hope they happen randomly her herd virtural cats to make it happen.
A planned story means looking ahead to make sure requirements can be met. The most common play to
play a story is by hand. Script for Triple-A games exceed the length of the Bible today but are still
limited to what can be image imagined in advance. By the way, these pictures are a couple prototypes
we built where the story is planned and replanned by an algorithm while the game is running.
Planning means the stories and characters are anticipating future events. It might be one
ahead or several events and that's called reactive planning. The alternative is a search algorithm
that considers all possible event sequences of any length. Search is the most flexible kind but
the most expensive because there is billions and trillions and even infinite numbers. It is largely
doing reactive planning though it can maintain some long term reasoning in its context vector. I
will not say much about LLMs in this talk but come pack to them at the end. We are making stories out
of events which is about one sentence of content. There are preconditions and effects that change
the world in some way. You might have seen story lids which are pretty much the same thing but it
might be more like a scene than an event. A planner is an algorithm that starts in the
initial state of your story world and finds all events whose preconditions are met and simulates
what the world would be like if you did those and then finds events that could happen next
and simulates those until we find a state where the story is over usually that means the player
died or achieved their goal. A planner considers everything that could possible that could happen
and chooses one story to make a good story. You could use a deterministic decision plan. You
start in the initial state, it finds a sequence of events that achieve the goal. Classical planning
algorithms have been around since the 1960s and every year cool researchers find new ways to make
them faster. The downside is you have to write a lot of story context in the preconditions. I could
say only rogues steal things and only things they want. The other options is specialized planning
that has knowledge built in. The cool thing about a story planner is you write the basic conditions
of the event. It is up to the planner who can steal and what they can steal. The algorithm looks
for context when it makes sense. This saves effort and adds flexibility but it means they need a
model of what counts as a good story. A classical planner can put Lego bricks any way they fit so it
is up to you that they always look good. A story planner will only put the bricks together in a
way that makes sense but this means they need a definition of when a story makes sense and that's
pretty complicated. This talk is about the last 25 years of story planning research where we have
been asking the question how do you represent a story on a computer. We start in 1999 with this
paper by my PhD advisor Michael young who suggests using a planning algorithm to write and rewrite
the story in a game. The classical planner will generate every vent that can get you to the end
but plots of plans are not good stories is the problem and we are about to see that. I will show
you definitions of a story followed by examples of how they don't work. The best part of the
1997' paper is the misspuned tales which we lists the funny outputs. We come up with a definition,
try it out, sometimes it works but most of the time it shows us new problems and those problems
motivate the next steps in the research. Here is a simple story from one of the prototypes we built.
Your grandmother is sick. Gives you her very last coin. You set off on a quest for medicine.
Thankfully there is a merchant at the market who has some for sale. If you let a classical planner
write the storea you might get something like this. The merchant walks to your house and hands
you the medicine. That's a sequence of events that ends in success but doesn't make sense. They don't
magically know what you want or give things away for free. The first story planner was made to fix
this. It had intentionality. A good story is still a sequence of events that achieves the
story's goal but every action needs to attribute to achieving some character goal. We ruled out the
merchant bringing the story but we can still tell the story where you went to buy it. Intentions get
propagated backward. We can simulate the walking to the market and not sure why, simulate buying
the medicine but not sure, we see the players goal was achieved and this explains the other
actions he did that contributed to the last event. We can meet the merchant's reasoning for selling.
We can explain why every character did what they did based on their goals. The trouble with this
first story planner was it didn't allow character plans to fail. Imagine our story world also had an
armed bandit and on the way to the market to get the medicine the bandit finds you and steals your
money. Stories usually resolve around conflict so we would want to tell this but we don't have an ex
planation of why you would walk to the crossroads. We are still generating one story from start to
finish and propagating explanations backwards. The bandit robs you because they want money and
walk to the crossroads so they can Rob you but we can't come up with an explanation for why the
player would walk to the crossroads. Doesn't make sense to say you walked to the crossroads so you
could get Robbed but actually you were hoping to continue on to the market to buy the medicine but
that plan got interrupted. We can still use that plan as an explanation for an action. A
planner is generating millions of stories before it settles on one. All the other stories it didn't
use aren't just wasted effort. They are a useful database of other possible stories that could have
happened instead. The definition of a story is a little broader instead of saying actions only
make sense when they are part of a character plan that Werbs we relax that and say an action makes
sense if there exist a story where it makes sense even if that isn't the story you actually end up
telling. We could have told the story where you walk to the market and buy the medicine or where
the bandit ross Robs you. The fact it was possible let's it be explained and how this robbery story
still makes sense. We have made some good progress but we are still generate aglot of misspun tales.
Suppose there is a guard stationed at the market whose job is to punish law breakers. You are on
the way, get Robbed, and the guard charges in from off screen to slay the bandit. How did the
guard know about this because he wasn't around? The problem is planners assume full observability
which means everybody knows about everything accurately as soon as it happens. We developed
the saber story planner to reason about character beliefs and broad ns the definition of a story to
reason about plans characters think are possible even if they really aren't. When we are trying to
explain by a character does something they have to have a plan they think will work to achieve their
goals based on what they know and have observed. We aren't done yet. Say you are on the way to the
market, get Robbed, the guard won't come running because he doesn't know about the robbery,
what does the bandit do next? Runs off the market to Rob the merchant. The bandit isn't anticipating
what the guard will do when she shows up at the market. Hope means finding a plan to achieve your
goals what we were already doing. Now we can reason about fear which means imaging a plan
other characters might do that will be bad for you and relief which means a plan that prevents a
fear from happening. This paper also defines other emotions as well as personality types so a risky
bandit might go for a second score in the market despite the guard but a careful bandit would avoid
the market. We are broadening the definition of a good story saying characters should only form
plans they believe will lead to a positive emotion like achieving the goal. The bandit won't go go to
the market because she doesn't want to risk it. We originally designed the guard in this game to
be hungry imaging ways you could get him to leave the post or entice him with poisoned food. Every
time we tested this we would show up and the guard was already dead. While on the way, it
turns out the guard would steal food, eat it and then attack himself because he is a criminal. The
story as a whole doesn't make sense because he is not reasoning about the relative importance
of his goals. Our latest paper we are presenting in a few weeks narrows the definition of a good
story back down to only consider plans on each characters parato front. It is on that front
when there is no better plan that is better in some way without being worse in some way.
Suppose a character told you they love pizza and pepperoni is their favorite. You go out with them
and they order a slice of these. Does that make sense? They love pizza so it makes sense but like
pepperoni more so it doesn't seem realistic. Ordering pepperoni is strictly better so it is
on the front and ordering cheese is not. Suppose you heard there is a Listeria outbreak affecting
pepperoni and now pepperoni is better but cheese is safer. In other words, when we ask if an action
makes sense we have the consider the other choices a character could have made. A plan only makes
sense if there was no other plan that was better in some ways without being worse. In summary,
a story planner is a search algorithm considering every possible sequence of events until it finds
one that can achieve the story's goal goal. The character believes it will achieve a positive
emotion. And there is no other plan they could have picked which is better in one way without
also being worse in a different way. What about replanning? If you can quickly plan a good story,
you can replan it when the player does something unexpected. If the player is
about to do something that will make telling the story impossible you stop them from doing it.
We call that intervention. Ideally you let the player do what they want and replan around the
action called accommodation. There are fancier method in these papers if you are interested.
The last question which I don't time to go into is whether we can do story time planning fast
enough at run-time. We probably need billions of sequences. We can generate stories on the order
of 5-10 events depending on a lot of factors. We have done a lot of research on speeding up
story planning. One is fancy heuristics. In this paper we developed a heuristic that develops a
sketch of what it thinks the rest of the story looks like and uses that as a guide. We can use
fancy methods with or without heuristics. We can try to only build plans where each events
satisfy preconditions of an vent after. We can reason about which people, places and goals are
salient in the player's working memory and only allow events that involve those salient elements.
And you might think large language models might be good at a story planner. They don't have to write
that. Surprisingly they are not better at this than older heuristic methods. Language models
are pretty good at open ended storytelling but struggle with long term story planning. Though,
that's starting to improve with the so-called thinking models. I didn't talk much about LLM
because I wanted to focus on the definition of a story and it is hard to get one to follow
the formal definition. If you are interested though check out this paper for an example of
the hilarious spins you get. There has been cool work on getting LLMs to plan stories better by
making them first generate and fill out outlines. And a research group at Georgia tech has done
research on using LLM for structured storytelling. Story planning has allowed us to make a few cool
research prototypes. Our most recent one was a virtual reality police de-escalation training
system. We have specific content we need the story to include and we need to make sure you
get a good ending when you do the right thing and a bad ending when you do the wrong thing. We need
you to understand why the wrong thing led to the bad ending so we want a fully deterministic story
with no randomness because we want you to replay it, intentionally do something different, and see
how that leads to a better ending. We need the storytelling engine to look ahead and make sure
it is always possible to tell the story we want to tell. We want them to have hope, fear and relief
and complies the best available plan. -- choose. Is a training simulation a roguelike?
It is meant to be repeated and it has permadeath but not much in the level generation. Come chat
with me if you want to fight with me about this at break. This has been a quick talk on 25 years.
To sum up the big lessons I think storytelling is really need because it lets you look ated to
ensure the story you need to tell is possible. However it is really complicated. One reason is
because storytelling is non-mar covian meaning you can't reason whether an event makes sense just by
looking at the current state. You need the whole sequence of events, past and future, to decide
whether an event makes sense. You can't just say whether an event contributes to a character's
goal unless you know what they did before and are planning to do next and sometimes you need to know
all the other things that could have happened instead. To know if a plan is the best one to
choose you have to look at all the other ones they could have done. We can only judge the quality of
a story relative to the other stories we could have told. Generating and checking all these
is really expensive. Given how successful story planners are, I am optimistic we will see cool
planned interactive experiences in video games and maybe even in a roguelike. Thank for listening.
